'''Per H. Enflo''' ({{IPA|sv|ˈpæːr ˈěːnfluː|lang}}; born 20 May 1944) is a Swedish mathematician working primarily in [[functional analysis]], a field in which he solved [[mathematical problems|problems]] that had been considered fundamental. Three of these problems had been [[open problem|open]] for more than forty years:<ref>Page 586 in Halmos 1990.</ref>
* The [[Schauder basis#Basis problem|basis problem]] and the [[Approximation property|approximation problem]]<ref>Per Enflo: ''A counterexample to the approximation problem in Banach spaces.'' [[Acta Mathematica]] vol. 130, no. 1, Juli 1973</ref> and later
* the [[invariant subspace problem]] for [[Banach spaces]].<ref>*{{Cite book | last1=Enflo | first1=Per | title=Séminaire Maurey--Schwartz (1975--1976) Espaces L<sup>p</sup>, applications radonifiantes et géométrie des espaces de Banach, Exp. Nos. 14-15 | publisher=Centre Math., École Polytech., Palaiseau | mr=0473871 | year=1976 | chapter=On the invariant subspace problem in Banach spaces | page=7}}
* {{Cite journal | last1=Enflo | first1=Per | title=On the invariant subspace problem for Banach spaces | doi=10.1007/BF02392260 | mr=892591 | year=1987 | journal=[[Acta Mathematica]] | issn=0001-5962 | volume=158 | issue=3 | pages=213–313| doi-access=free }}
</ref>

In solving these problems, Enflo developed new techniques which were then used by other researchers in [[functional analysis]] and [[operator theory]] for years. Some of Enflo's research has been important also in other mathematical fields, such as [[number theory]], and in [[computer science]], especially [[computer algebra]] and [[approximation algorithm]]s.

Enflo works at [[Kent State University]], where he holds the title of University Professor. Enflo has earlier held positions at the [[Miller Institute]] for Basic Research in Science at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], [[Stanford University]], [[École Polytechnique]], ([[Paris]]) and The [[Royal Institute of Technology]], [[Stockholm]].

Enflo is also a [[concert pianist]].

== Enflo's contributions to functional analysis and operator theory ==

In [[mathematical analysis|mathematics]], [[functional analysis]] is concerned with the study of [[vector space]]s and [[Operator (mathematics)|operators]] acting upon them. It has its historical roots in the study of [[functional space]]s, in particular transformations of [[function (mathematics)|functions]], such as the [[Fourier transform]], as well as in the study of [[differential equations|differential]] and [[integral equations|integral]] equations. In functional analysis, an important class of vector spaces consists of the [[complete space|complete]] [[normed vector space]]s over the [[real number|real]] or [[complex number|complex]] numbers, which are called [[Banach space]]s. An important example of a Banach space is a [[Hilbert space]], where the [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] arises from an [[inner product space|inner product]]. Hilbert spaces are of fundamental importance in many areas, including the mathematical formulation of [[quantum mechanics]], [[stochastic processes]], and [[time-series analysis]]. Besides studying spaces of functions, functional analysis also studies the [[continuous function (topology)|continuous]] [[linear transformation|linear operators]] on spaces of functions.

=== Hilbert's fifth problem and embeddings ===
{{see also|Hilbert's fifth problem}}

At Stockholm University, Hans Rådström suggested that Enflo consider [[Hilbert's fifth problem]] in the spirit of functional analysis.<ref>Rådström had himself published several articles on [[Hilbert's fifth problem]] from the point of view of [[semigroup]] theory.
Rådström was also the (initial) advisor of Martin Ribe, who wrote a thesis on metric linear spaces that need not be locally convex; Ribe also used a few of Enflo's ideas on [[metric geometry]], especially "roundness", in obtaining independent results on [[uniformly continuous function|uniform]] and [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz]] [[embedding]]s (Benyamini and Lindenstrauss). This reference also describes results of Enflo and his students on such embeddings.</ref> In two years, 1969–1970, Enflo published five papers on Hilbert's fifth problem; these papers are collected in Enflo (1970), along with a short summary. Some of the results of these papers are described in Enflo (1976) and in the last chapter of Benyamini and [[Joram Lindenstrauss|Lindenstrauss]].

==== Applications in computer science ====
{{See also|Approximation algorithm}}
Enflo's techniques have found application in [[computer science]]. [[Algorithm|Algorithm theorists]] derive [[approximation algorithm]]s that embed finite metric spaces into low-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]s with low "distortion" (in [[Mikhail Gromov (mathematician)|Gromov]]'s terminology for the [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz]] [[Category theory|category]]; cf. [[Banach–Mazur distance]]). Low-dimensional problems have lower [[Analysis of algorithms|computational complexity]], of course. More importantly, if the problems embed well in either the [[Euclidean plane]] or the three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]], then [[Computational geometry|geometric algorithms]] become exceptionally fast.

However, such [[embedding]] techniques have limitations, as shown by Enflo's (1969) theorem:<ref>Theorem 15.4.1 in Matoušek.</ref>
: For every <math>m\geq 2</math><!-- and <math>n=2^m</math>-->, the [[Hamming cube]] <math>C_m</math> cannot be embedded with "distortion <math>D</math>" (or less) into <math>2^m</math>-dimensional Euclidean space if <math> D < \sqrt{ m }</math>.<!-- \sqrt{ \log_2{ n } } = --> Consequently, the optimal embedding is the natural embedding, which realizes <math>\{0,1\}^m</math> as a subspace of <math>m</math>-dimensional Euclidean space.<ref>Matoušek 370.</ref>
This theorem, "found by Enflo [1969], is probably the first result showing an unbounded distortion for [[embedding]]s into [[Euclidean space]]s. Enflo considered the problem of [[uniform continuity|uniform]] embeddability among [[Banach space]]s, and the distortion was an auxiliary device in his proof."<ref>Matoušek 372.</ref>

=== Geometry of Banach spaces ===
{{see also|Uniformly convex space}}
A '''uniformly convex space''' is a [[Banach space]] so that, for every <math>\epsilon>0</math> there is some <math>\delta>0</math> so that for any two vectors with <math>\|x\|\le1</math> and <math>\|y\|\le 1,</math>
: <math>\|x+y\|>2-\delta</math>
implies that
: <math>\|x-y\|<\epsilon.</math>
Intuitively, the center of a line segment inside the [[unit ball]] must lie deep inside the unit ball unless the segment is short.

In 1972 Enflo proved that "every [[Reflexive space#Super-reflexive space|super-reflexive]] [[Banach space]] admits an equivalent [[uniformly convex space|uniformly convex]] norm".<ref>Beauzamy 1985, page 298.</ref><ref>Pisier.</ref>
<!-- Other results on convex geometry, like work with Beauzamy & Maurey; maybe on 3-space problems, etc. -->

=== The basis problem and Mazur's goose ===
{{see also|Schauder basis|Approximation problem}}

With one paper, which was published in 1973, Per Enflo solved three problems that had stumped functional analysts for decades: The [[approximation problem|basis problem]] of [[Stefan Banach]], the "[[Scottish Book|Goose problem]]" of [[Stanisław Mazur]], and the [[approximation problem]] of [[Alexander Grothendieck]]. Grothendieck had shown that his approximation problem was the central problem in the [[category theory|theory]] of [[Banach space]]s and [[continuous linear operator]]s.

==== Basis problem of Banach ====
{{Main|Schauder basis}}

{{See also|Stefan Banach|Banach space|Separable space}}
The basis problem was posed by Stefan Banach in his book, ''Theory of Linear Operators''. Banach asked whether every separable [[Banach space]] has a [[Schauder basis]].

A '''Schauder basis''' or '''countable basis''' is similar to the usual (Hamel) [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]] of a [[vector space]]; the difference is that for Hamel bases we use [[linear combination]]s that are ''finite'' sums, while for Schauder bases they may be ''infinite'' sums. This makes Schauder bases more suitable for the analysis of infinite-dimensional [[topological vector space]]s including [[Banach space]]s.

Schauder bases were described by [[Juliusz Schauder]] in 1927.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Schauder | first1 = J. |name-list-style=vanc | year = 1927 | title = Zur Theorie stetiger Abbildungen in Funktionalraumen | url =http://dml.cz/bitstream/handle/10338.dmlcz/104881/CommentatMathUnivCarol_001-1960-4_4.pdf | journal = Mathematische Zeitschrift | volume = 26 | pages = 47–65 | doi = 10.1007/BF01475440 | hdl = 10338.dmlcz/104881 | s2cid = 123042807 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Schauder | first1 = J. |name-list-style=vanc | year = 1928 | title = Eine Eigenschaft des Haarschen Orthogonalsystems | journal = Mathematische Zeitschrift | volume = 28 | pages = 317–320 | doi = 10.1007/BF01181164 | s2cid = 120228356 }}</ref> Let ''V'' denote a [[Banach space]] over the [[field (mathematics)|field]] ''F''. A ''Schauder basis'' is a [[sequence]] (''b''<sub>''n''</sub>) of elements of ''V'' such that for every element ''v'' ∈ ''V'' there exists a ''unique'' sequence (α<sub>''n''</sub>) of elements in ''F'' so that
: <math> v = \sum_{n \in \N} \alpha_n b_n \,</math>
where the [[Series (mathematics)#Series in Banach and seminormed spaces|convergence]] is understood with respect to the [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] [[topology]]. Schauder bases can also be defined analogously in a general [[topological vector space]].

[[File:KsiegaSzkocka1.JPG|thumb |In 1937, Polish mathematician [[Stanisław Mazur]] promised a "live goose" as the prize for solving [[approximation problem|problem 153]] in the [[Scottish Book]]. In 1972, Mazur presented the goose to Per Enflo. ]]

==== Problem 153 in the Scottish Book: Mazur's goose ====
[[File:MazurGes.jpg|thumb|right|In 1972 [[Stanisław Mazur]] awarded Enflo the promised live goose for solving a problem in the [[Scottish cafe|Scottish book]].]]
{{See also|Scottish Café|Scottish Book|Stanisław Mazur}}

Banach and other Polish mathematicians would work on mathematical problems at the [[Scottish Café]]. When a problem was especially interesting and when its solution seemed difficult, the problem would be written down in the book of problems, which soon became known as the ''[[Scottish Book]]''. For problems that seemed especially important or difficult or both, the problem's proposer would often pledge to award a prize for its solution.

On 6 November 1936, [[Stanisław Mazur]] posed a problem on representing continuous functions. Formally writing down ''problem 153'' in the ''Scottish Book'', Mazur promised as the reward a "live [[goose]]", an especially rich prize during the [[Great Depression]] and on the eve of [[World War II]].

Fairly soon afterwards, it was realized that Mazur's problem was closely related to Banach's problem on the existence of Schauder bases in separable Banach spaces. Most of the other problems in the ''Scottish Book'' were solved regularly. However, there was little progress on Mazur's problem and a few other problems, which became famous [[open problem]]s to mathematicians around the world.<ref>Mauldin</ref>

==== Grothendieck's formulation of the approximation problem ====
{{Main|Approximation property|Approximation problem}}

{{See also|Compact operator|Alexander Grothendieck}}

Grothendieck's work on the [[category theory|theory]] of Banach spaces and [[continuous linear operator]]s introduced the [[approximation property]]. A [[Banach space]] is said to have the [[approximation property]], if every [[compact operator]] is a limit of [[finite-rank operator]]s. The converse is always true.<ref name="ReferenceA">[[Joram Lindenstrauss]] and L. Tzafriri.</ref>

In a long monograph, Grothendieck proved that if every Banach space had the approximation property, then every Banach space would have a Schauder basis. Grothendieck thus focused the attention of functional analysts on deciding whether every Banach space have the approximation property.<ref name="ReferenceA" />

==== Enflo's solution ====
In 1972, Per Enflo constructed a separable Banach space that lacks the approximation property and a Schauder basis.<ref>Enflo's "sensation" is discussed on page 287 in {{cite book|last=Pietsch|first=Albrecht|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MMorKHumdZAC&q=enflo&pg=PA203 |title=History of Banach spaces and linear operators|publisher=Birkhäuser Boston, Inc.|location=Boston, MA|year=2007|pages=xxiv+855 pp|isbn=978-0-8176-4367-6| mr = 2300779}} Introductions to Enflo's solution were written by Halmos, by Johnson, by Kwapień, by Lindenstrauss and Tzafriri, by Nedevski and Trojanski, and by Singer.</ref> In 1972, Mazur awarded a [http://www.apprendre-math.info/history/photos/Mazur_2.jpeg live goose] to Enflo in a ceremony at the [[Stefan Banach|Stefan Banach Center]] in [[Warsaw, Poland|Warsaw]]; the "goose reward" ceremony was broadcast throughout [[Poland]].<ref>Kałuża, Saxe, Eggleton, Mauldin.</ref>

=== Invariant subspace problem and polynomials ===
{{main|Invariant subspace problem}}
 {{see also|Invariant subspace}}

In [[functional analysis]], one of the most prominent problems was the [[invariant subspace problem]], which required the evaluation of the truth of the following proposition:
:Given a complex [[Banach space]] ''H'' of [[dimension (vector space)|dimension]] > 1 and a [[bounded operator|bounded linear operator]] ''T''&nbsp;:&nbsp;''H''&nbsp;→&nbsp;''H'', then ''H'' has a non-trivial [[closed set|closed]] [[invariant subspace|''T''-invariant subspace]], i.e. there exists a closed [[linear subspace]] ''W'' of ''H'' which is different from {0} and ''H'' such that ''T''(''W'') ⊆ ''W''.
For [[Banach space]]s, the first example of an operator without an invariant subspace was constructed by Enflo. (For [[Hilbert space]]s, the [[invariant subspace problem]] remains [[Unsolved problems in mathematics|open]].)

Enflo proposed a solution to the invariant subspace problem in 1975, publishing an outline in 1976. Enflo submitted the full article in 1981 and the article's complexity and length delayed its publication to 1987<ref name="Beauzamy 1988; Yadav">Beauzamy 1988; Yadav.</ref> Enflo's long "manuscript had a world-wide circulation among mathematicians"<ref>Yadav, page 292.</ref> and some of its ideas were described in publications besides Enflo (1976).<ref>For example, Radjavi and Rosenthal (1982).</ref><ref>
{{cite journal
|pages=33–37
|author1=Heydar Radjavi  |author2=Peter Rosenthal
 |name-list-style=amp |title=The invariant subspace problem
|journal=The Mathematical Intelligencer
|volume=4
|issue=1
|date=March 1982
|doi=10.1007/BF03022994
|s2cid=122811130 |url=https://arcabc.ca/islandora/object/tru%3A1187 }}
</ref> Enflo's works inspired a similar construction of an operator without an invariant subspace for example by Beauzamy, who acknowledged Enflo's ideas.<ref name="Beauzamy 1988; Yadav" />

In the 1990s, Enflo developed a "constructive" approach to the [[invariant subspace problem]] on Hilbert spaces.<ref>Page 401 in {{cite journal|last1=Foiaş|first1=Ciprian|last2=Jung|first2=Il Bong|last3=Ko|first3=Eungil|last4=Pearcy|first4=Carl | title=On quasinilpotent operators. III | journal=Journal of Operator Theory | volume=54|year=2005|issue=2|pages=401–414}}. Enflo's method of ("forward") "minimal vectors" is also noted in the review of this research article by Gilles Cassier in ''[[Mathematical Reviews]]'': {{MR|2186363}}

Enflo's method of minimal vector is described in greater detail in a survey article on the [[invariant subspace problem]] by Enflo and [[Invariant subspace problem|Victor Lomonosov]], which appears in the ''Handbook of the Geometry of Banach Spaces'' (2001).</ref>

==== Multiplicative inequalities for homogeneous polynomials ====
{{see also|homogeneous polynomial}}

An essential idea in Enflo's construction was "'''concentration of polynomials at low degrees'''": For all positive integers <math>m</math> and <math>n</math>, there exists <math>C(m,n) > 0 </math> such that for all [[homogeneous polynomial]]s <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math> of degrees <math>m</math> and <math>n</math> (in <math>k</math> variables), then
<blockquote><math>|PQ|\geq C(m,n)|P|\,|Q|,</math></blockquote>
where <math>|P|</math> denotes the sum of the absolute values of the coefficients of <math>P</math>. Enflo proved that <math>C(m,n)</math> does not depend on the number of variables <math>k</math>. Enflo's original proof was simplified by [[Hugh Montgomery (mathematician)|Montgomery]].<ref>Schmidt, page 257.</ref>

This result was generalized to other [[normed vector space|norms]] on the vector space of [[homogeneous polynomial]]s. Of these norms, the most used has been the [[Bombieri norm]].

===== Bombieri norm =====
{{main|Bombieri norm}}

The [[Bombieri norm]] is defined in terms of the following [[scalar product]]:
For all <math> \alpha,\beta \in \mathbb{N}^N</math> we have

: <math>\langle X^\alpha | X^\beta \rangle = 0</math> if <math>\alpha \neq \beta</math>

: For every <math> \alpha \in \mathbb{N}^N</math> we define <math>\Vert X^\alpha\Vert^2 = \frac{|\alpha|!}{\alpha!},</math>
where we use the following notation:
if <math>\alpha = (\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_N) \in \mathbb{N}^N</math>, we write <math>|\alpha| = \Sigma_{i=1}^N \alpha_i</math> and
<math>\alpha! = \Pi_{i=1}^N (\alpha_i!)</math> and <math>X^\alpha = \Pi_{i=1}^N X_i^{\alpha_i}.</math>

The most remarkable property of this norm is the Bombieri inequality:

Let <math>P,Q</math> be two [[homogeneous polynomial]]s respectively of degree <math>d^\circ(P)</math> and <math>d^\circ(Q)</math> with <math>N</math> variables, then, the following inequality holds:

: <math>\frac{d^\circ(P)!d^\circ(Q)!}{(d^\circ(P)+d^\circ(Q))!}\Vert P\Vert^2 \, \Vert Q\Vert^2 \leq
 \Vert P\cdot Q\Vert^2 \leq \Vert P\Vert^2 \, \Vert Q\Vert^2.</math>

In the above statement, the Bombieri inequality is the left-hand side inequality; the right-hand side inequality means that the [[Bombieri norm]] is a [[normed algebra|norm]] of the [[normed algebra|algebra]] of polynomials under multiplication.

The Bombieri inequality implies that the product of two polynomials cannot be arbitrarily small, and this lower-bound is fundamental in applications like [[polynomial factorization]] (or in Enflo's construction of an operator without an invariant subspace).

==== Applications ====
{{see also|Polynomial factorization}}
Enflo's idea of "concentration of polynomials at low degrees" has led to important publications in [[number theory]]<ref>Montgomery. Schmidt. Beauzamy and Enflo. Beauzamy, Bombieri, Enflo, and Montgomery</ref> [[algebraic geometry|algebraic]] [[Diophantine geometry|and Diophantine geometry]],<ref>Bombieri and Gubler</ref> and [[polynomial factorization]].<ref>Knuth. Beauzamy, Enflo, and Wang.</ref>

== Mathematical biology: Population dynamics ==
{{See also|Mathematical biology|Population dynamics}}

In [[applied mathematics]], Per Enflo has published several papers in [[mathematical biology]], specifically in [[population dynamics]].

=== Human evolution ===
Enflo has also published in [[population genetics]] and [[paleoanthropology]].<ref>The model for the evolution of human population genetics (developed by Enflo and his coauthors) was reported on the cover page of a major Swedish newspaper.{{cite journal | first=Annika | last=Jensfelt | page=1 |title=Ny brandfackla tänder debatten om manniskans ursprung | newspaper=[[Svenska Dagbladet]] |language=Swedish |  date=14 January 2001}}</ref>

Today, all humans belong to one population of ''[[Homo sapiens sapiens]]'', which is individed by species barrier. However, according to the "Out of Africa" model this is not the first species of hominids: the first species of genus ''Homo'', ''[[Homo habilis]]'', evolved in [[East Africa]] at least 2 Ma, and members of this species populated different parts of Africa in a relatively short time. ''[[Homo erectus]]'' evolved more than 1.8 Ma, and by 1.5 Ma had spread throughout the [[Old World]].

[[Anthropology|Anthropologists]] have been divided as to whether the current human population evolved as one interconnected population (as postulated by the [[Multiregional Evolution]] hypothesis), or evolved only in East Africa, where they [[speciation|speciated]], then migrated out of Africa, replacing human populations in [[Eurasia]] (referred to as the "Out of Africa" Model or the "Complete Replacement" Model).

[[Neanderthal]]s and modern humans coexisted in Europe for several thousand years, but the duration of this period is uncertain.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Mellars | first1 = P. | year = 2006 | title = A new radiocarbon revolution and the dispersal of modern humans in Eurasia | journal = Nature | volume = 439 | issue = 7079| pages = 931–935 | doi = 10.1038/nature04521 | pmid = 16495989 | bibcode=2006Natur.439..931M| s2cid = 4416359 }}</ref> Modern humans may have first migrated to Europe 40–43,000 years ago.<ref name=banks>{{cite journal|last=Banks|first=William E. |author2=Francesco d'Errico |author3=A. Townsend Peterson |author4=Masa Kageyama |author5=Adriana Sima |author6=Maria-Fernanda Sánchez-Goñi |date=24 December 2008|editor1-last=Harpending|editor1-first=Henry|title=Neanderthal Extinction by Competitive Exclusion|journal=PLOS ONE|publisher=Public Library of Science|volume=3|issue=12|article-number=e3972|issn=1932-6203 |doi=10.1371/journal.pone.0003972|pmid=19107186|pmc=2600607|bibcode = 2008PLoSO...3.3972B |doi-access=free }}</ref> Neanderthals may have lived as recently as 24,000 years ago in [[Refugium (population biology)|refugia]] on the south coast of the Iberian peninsula such as [[Gorham's Cave]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/1/hi/5343266.stm?lsm|title=Neanderthals' 'last rock refuge'|last=Rincon|first=Paul|date=13 September 2006|work=BBC News|access-date=2009-10-11}}</ref><ref>Finlayson, C., F. G. Pacheco, J. Rodriguez-Vidal, D. A. Fa, J. M. G. Lopez, A. S. Perez, G. Finlayson, E. Allue, J. B. Preysler, I. Caceres, J. S. Carrion, Y. F. Jalvo, C. P. Gleed-Owen, F. J. J. Espejo, P. Lopez, J. A. L. Saez, J. A. R. Cantal, A. S. Marco, F. G. Guzman, K. Brown, N. Fuentes, C. A. Valarino, A. Villalpando, C. B. Stringer, F. M. Ruiz, and T. Sakamoto. 2006. Late survival of Neanderthals at the southernmost extreme of Europe. ''Nature'' advanced online publication.</ref> Inter-stratification of Neanderthal and modern human remains has been suggested,<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Gravina | first1 = B. | last2 = Mellars | first2 = P. | last3 = Ramsey | first3 = C. B. | year = 2005 | title = Radiocarbon dating of interstratified Neanderthal and early modern human occupations at the Chatelperronian type-site | journal = Nature | volume = 438 | issue = 7064| pages = 51–56 | doi = 10.1038/nature04006 | pmid = 16136079 | bibcode=2005Natur.438...51G| s2cid = 4335868 }}</ref> but is disputed.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Zilhão|first=João |author2=Francesco d'Errico |author3=Jean-Guillaume Bordes |author4=Arnaud Lenoble |author5=Jean-Pierre Texier |author6=Jean-Philippe Rigaud|year=2006|title=Analysis of Aurignacian interstratification at the Châtelperronian-type site and implications for the behavioral modernity of Neandertals|journal=PNAS|volume=103|issue=33|pages=12643–12648 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0605128103|pmid=16894152|pmc=1567932|bibcode=2006PNAS..10312643Z|doi-access=free }}</ref>

With [[John D. Hawks|Hawks]] and [[Milford H. Wolpoff|Wolpoff]], Enflo published an explanation of fossil evidence on the [[DNA]] of [[Neanderthal]] and [[modern human]]s. This article tries to resolve a debate in the [[human evolution#Models of human evolution|evolution of modern humans]] between theories suggesting either [[multiregional origin of modern humans|multiregional]] and [[recent African origin of modern humans|single African]] origins. In particular,
the [[Neanderthal extinction hypotheses|extinction of Neanderthals]] could have happened due to waves of modern humans entered Europe&nbsp;– in technical terms, due to "the continuous influx of modern human DNA into the Neandertal gene pool."<ref>Page 665:

Enflo has also written about the population dynamics of [[zebra mussels]] in [[Lake Erie]].<ref>Saxe</ref>

== Piano ==
Per Enflo is also a [[concert pianist]].

A [[child prodigy]]<!-- Zimmerman states that Enflo was a child prodigy in mathematics, also. There were Swedish newspaper articles with titles like "Sweden's answer to Einstein". --> in both music and mathematics, Enflo won the Swedish competition for young pianists at age 11 in 1956, and he won the same competition in 1961.<ref>Saxe.</ref> At age 12, Enflo appeared as a soloist with the Royal Opera Orchestra of Sweden. He debuted in the [[Stockholm Concert Hall]] in 1963. Enflo's teachers included [[Bruno Seidlhofer]], [[Géza Anda]], and Gottfried Boon (who himself was a student of [[Artur Schnabel]]).<ref name="content.bandzoogle.com">* [http://content.bandzoogle.com/users/chagrinmusic/files/09-10-Season-Brochure_FINAL.pdf Chagrin Valley Chamber Music Concert Series 2009-2010] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121111064411/http://content.bandzoogle.com/users/chagrinmusic/files/09-10-Season-Brochure_FINAL.pdf |date=2012-11-11 }}.</ref>

In 1999 Enflo competed in the first annual [[Van Cliburn Foundation]]'s [[Van Cliburn International Piano Competition|International Piano Competition]] for [http://www.cliburn.org/index.php?page=amateur_competition Outstanding Amateurs] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090419114604/http://www.cliburn.org/index.php?page=amateur_competition |date=2009-04-19 }}.<ref>{{cite journal
|title=Prodigy's Return
|author=Michael Kimmelman
|journal=[[The New York Times Magazine]]
|date=August 8, 1999
|at=Section 6, p. 30
|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1999/08/08/magazine/prodigy-s-return.html?pagewanted=2
|author-link=Michael Kimmelman
}}
</ref>

Enflo performs regularly around [[Kent, Ohio|Kent]] and in a [[Mozart]] series in [[Columbus, Ohio]] (with the Triune Festival Orchestra). His solo piano recitals have appeared on the Classics Network of the radio station [[WOSU-FM|WOSU]], which is sponsored by [[Ohio State University]].<ref name="content.bandzoogle.com" />
